lines.text: Do you need care [zorg]?
In the Netherlands you always go first to the GP/family doctor [huisarts].
The huisarts can refer [doorverwijzen] you or knows where you can ask for help.
You can also get information about care from the gemeente and other organisations [organisaties].
Choosing a huisarts.
Have you just moved to the Netherlands, or have you recently moved house?
Then you first have to find a GP practice [huisartsenpraktijk].
You can find one on the internet, or ask other people for advice.
Not satisfied?
Then you can change to another practice [praktijk].
You ask whether the new practice will accept [accepteren] you as a patient.
Sometimes they don't accept you, for example if you live too far away or if there is no room.
You let the old practice know that you are leaving, and you ask them to send your medical file [dossier] to the new practice.
At the huisarts.
With physical complaints [lichamelijke klachten], but also with mental/psychological [psychische] complaints, you go first to the huisarts.
During an appointment you describe your complaints.
If necessary, the huisarts examines [onderzoekt] you.
Sometimes you get medicines.
Often the huisarts says: "It will go away by itself and you can take paracetamol."
The team in the practice.
The huisarts works in a team:
The doctor's assistant [doktersassistent] is the first person you get on the phone.
The assistant also helps with small problems, for example testing your urine or doing a blood pressure measurement [bloeddruk meten].
The GP practice support worker [POH, praktijkondersteuner huisarts] helps with mild mental complaints.
There you can talk about your complaints five to ten times.
You can also go to the praktijkondersteuner for a chronic [chronische] illness such as diabetes.
Referral.
The huisarts can refer you to a specialist in the hospital.
Without a referral [verwijzing] you cannot make an appointment with a specialist in the Netherlands.
With mental complaints you first talk to a POH; if that does not help, you can get a referral to mental health care [geestelijke gezondheidszorg, GGZ], for example a therapist [therapeut].
You can go to the physiotherapist [fysiotherapeut] on your own, without a referral.
With a referral you sometimes first end up on a waiting list [wachtlijst].
Medicines.
The huisarts can prescribe [voorschrijven] medicines and sends a prescription [recept] to the pharmacy [apotheek].
Many medicines, for example antibiotics [antibiotica], you can only get with a prescription.
Paracetamol you can buy without a prescription: at the pharmacy, the drugstore [drogist] and often also the supermarket.
Professional confidentiality and files.
Everyone who works in health care has professional/medical confidentiality [beroepsgeheim].
No one may simply pass on [doorgeven] medical information to others — that is only allowed with your consent [toestemming].
You can view your own file online; for that you need a Dutch digital ID [DigiD].
The language.
Don't you speak Dutch or English well?
You can bring an adult who speaks Dutch well.
You also have the right [recht] to an interpreter [tolk]: together with the doctor you call the interpreter centre [tolkencentrum] and get an interpreter on the phone.
An interpreter is free for the doctor and the patient.
The dentist.
You can choose your own dental practice [tandartsenpraktijk] (there does have to be room).
On the phone you often first get a dental assistant [tandartsassistent].
Dental hygienists [Mondhygiënisten] also work in the practice: they thoroughly clean your teeth [gebit], which keeps your teeth and gums [tandvlees] healthy.
Usually you go to the dental hygienist once or twice a year.
Even without complaints you go to the dentist for a check-up [controle]: at least once a year, usually twice.
Sometimes the dentist takes X-rays [röntgenfoto's].
Do you have a cavity?
Then a treatment [behandeling] is needed.
